summary:
Finland does not criminalise trans people or consensual sexual activity. Same-sex sexual activity has been legal since 1971, the age of consent was equalised at 16 in 1999, homosexuality was declassified as an illness in 1981, and transvestism was declassified as an illness in 2011. Discrimination on grounds of sexual orientation became a criminal offence in 1995, and discrimination on grounds of gender identity became a criminal offence in 2005.

Legal gender recognition was reformed by a law that took effect in 2023. The age limit is 18, down from a proposal to allow the change at 15 with guardian permission, and an applicant must observe a 30-day reflection period, with a limit of one change per year. Until April 2023 an applicant had to be sterilised or otherwise infertile and to hold a mental disorder diagnosis.

Finland was one of three countries, with the Netherlands and Sweden, that wrote infertility requirements explicitly into law for legal gender recognition. An investigation published on 10 September 2025 counted at least 11,000 people subjected to such conditions across the six countries it examined, and recorded that the last requirement in that group was phased out at the end of June 2025. Finland's own statutory sterilisation-era requirement ended with the 2023 reform, and the cohort that lived under it is documented.

Section 8(1) of the Discrimination Act prohibits discrimination on grounds including sexual orientation and other personal characteristics, whether the discrimination is based on fact or on assumption, with gender identity and expression covered since 2005. The Act on Equality between Women and Men covers sex and gender identity, and Parliament amended it in 2014 to extend its protections to employment, goods and services, education and health services.

The Police University College recorded 1,808 suspected hate-crime offences in its most recent reporting, the highest figure it has recorded, with defamation and assault the most common types. The sexual-orientation and gender-identity-or-expression category rose across the six reported years from 72 cases to 241, and the international review covering 2025 puts sexual orientation and gender identity among recurrent motives at 12% of cases. The Criminal Code contains no hate-crime offence, so motive is recorded only in police reports: incidents are counted as reported suspicions rather than charges.

Finnish police reported 73 violent attacks and assaults against LGBT people in 2018, a 27% increase on 2017 and the only hate-motive category to rise that year. In November 2019 the Institute of Health and Welfare reported that LGBT children and youth face significantly more bullying, physical, psychological and sexual violence than heterosexual peers, and are more likely to suffer violence at home.

Finland's first prosecution over conversion practices was brought as assault, with convictions in March. In March, Parliament endorsed a citizens'-initiative-backed ban on conversion practices by 125 votes to 49, while a full statutory ban remained pending at the close of the period covered by the review.

Gender-affirming care for minors is delivered through the country's two centralised gender identity units. In 2020 the Council for Choices in Health Care revised its clinical recommendations for gender dysphoria under age 25, prioritising psychosocial therapy over medical transition and restricting puberty blockers and hormone treatment. These are recommendations rather than mandates: puberty blockers remain available case by case, and cross-sex hormones can be considered where the identity is of a permanent nature causing severe dysphoria. A survey by the LGBTI organisation Seta found over 40% of trans respondents entirely unable to access the care they needed, most of them reporting extended waiting times.

Same-sex marriage and joint adoption became legal on 1 March 2017. Registered partnerships, available from 2002 until 1 March 2017, gave same-sex couples the rights of married couples except adoption and a joint surname, and gave immigration rights to a foreign same-sex partner. Stepchild adoption became legal in 2009. In February 2018 Parliament approved a change to the Maternity Act recognising both women in a same-sex partnership as mothers from the moment of the child's birth, fixing second-parent registration at birth rather than through adoption, and an April 2019 law passed 122 to 42 gave lesbian couples full maternity pay and parentage rights without intra-family adoption.
tangentialFactors:
On 21 March 2025 Finland updated its travel advice for its own transgender citizens travelling to the United States, following reports of border difficulties after that country's executive order declaring two genders. The advice is outbound guidance issued to Finland's own travellers and is not an assessment of risk within Finland.

The Finnish constitution allows a citizens' initiative carrying 50,000 valid signatures to be put to Parliament. That route produced both the same-sex marriage law that took effect in 2017 and the conversion-practices bill endorsed in March, so legislative change on these questions runs through direct citizen sponsorship rather than party programmes alone.

The hate-crime figures are raw counts of reported suspicions with no population denominator, and the Police University College notes that motive is not a category in the Criminal Code. Ranking Finnish regions or comparison countries on these raw counts would track reporting volume and population rather than per-capita risk.

Public visibility is high: the first public gay demonstration was held in 1981, a gay rights panel aired on the state broadcaster Yle TV2 in 2010, and an estimated 100,000 people attended Helsinki Pride in 2018.
localsOnly:
Support organisations operate nationwide: Seta, founded in 1974; Trasek, working on trans and intersex rights; and Rainbow Families. A gay scene of bars, clubs and cafés functions in Helsinki, and Pride events are held in numerous cities.

Since December 2023 there has been no additional deferral period on blood donation for men who have sex with men.

Legal gender recognition is administered domestically under the 2023 law, with the 30-day reflection period and the one-change-per-year limit applying to residents using the procedure.
outOfScopeNotes:
The sources disagree on the year of the 1,808 hate-crime figure: the international review dates it to 2025, while the Police University College release of November 2025 dates the same total to 2024. The discrepancy is unresolved here.

The end date of Finland's infertility requirement is not fully reconciled across sources: the 2023 reform removed the sterilisation and diagnosis conditions, while the investigation of 10 September 2025 places the phase-out of the last such requirement among six countries at the end of June 2025. Whether that later date refers to Finland or to another of the six is not stated.

The Seta survey finding that over 40% of trans respondents could not access needed care gives no field period, so its currency cannot be dated.

No trans-specific killing rate or trans-specific violence rate appears in this inventory. The 2018 assault count and the 2019 Institute of Health and Welfare findings are LGBT-wide, not trans-specific, and are stated with their dates only.

Entry and visa rules, passport and gender-marker handling at Finnish border control, airport screening of binders, packers or breast forms, and access to gendered facilities are not sourced in this inventory and remain unresolved.

The status of the conversion-practices ban after Parliament's March endorsement is not sourced beyond the review's statement that a full ban remained pending, and whether the 2020 recommendations on gender dysphoria under 25 have since been revised is likewise not sourced.
